body:
What does work mean in physics?

In everyday language, any activity requiring physical or mental effort may be called work. In physics, however, work has a specific meaning. Work is done on an object when a force acting on it causes displacement in the direction of the force or has a component along the displacement.

Consider a person pushing a loaded handcart. The person applies a force, and the cart moves. The force therefore does work on the cart. By contrast, a person may push a rigid wall with great effort without moving it. Although the person becomes tired, the work done by that force on the wall is zero because the wall has not been displaced.

Work: When a constant force acts in the direction of an object's displacement, the work done equals the product of the force and the displacement.

\(W=Fs\)

Here, \(W\) is work done, \(F\) is the magnitude of the constant force and \(s\) is the displacement in the direction of that force. This simple expression applies when the force and displacement are in the same direction. Their relative directions must be considered in other cases.

SI unit of work

The SI unit of force is the newton (N), and the SI unit of displacement is the metre (m). Consequently, the SI unit of work is the joule (J).

\(1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{N}\times1\,\mathrm{m}\)

One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N displaces an object by 1 m in the direction of that force. The joule is named after the physicist James Prescott Joule.

A simple calculation

A person pushes a cart with a constant horizontal force of 5 N. The cart moves 2 m horizontally in the direction of the force.

\(W=Fs=5\times2=10\,\mathrm{J}\)

The work done by the applied force is 10 J.

Positive, negative and zero work

Work is a scalar quantity: it has no direction of its own. Nevertheless, work done by a particular force can be positive, negative or zero because the direction of the force relative to displacement matters.

  • Positive work: A force acts in the direction of displacement. For example, the pushing force on a cart moving forward does positive work.
  • Negative work: A force acts opposite to displacement. For example, a braking force on a moving vehicle does negative work because it opposes the vehicle's motion.
  • Zero work: An object has no displacement, or the force is perpendicular to its displacement. For example, the vertical supporting force on a bag carried horizontally at constant height does zero work on the bag.

In the diagram, the object moves 2 m horizontally to the right. A constant 5 N force directed to the right does +10 J of work. A constant 5 N force directed to the left does −10 J of work. A constant 5 N force directed vertically does 0 J of work because it is perpendicular to the displacement.

Work must be identified with a particular force

Several forces may act on the same object simultaneously. Some may do positive work while others do negative work. For a cart moving at constant speed on a horizontal surface, the forward pulling force may do positive work while friction does negative work. These contributions can balance, making the net work zero even though individual forces have done nonzero work.

Similarly, a person holding a heavy object without moving it may consume chemical energy and become tired. This does not mean that the supporting force has done mechanical work on the stationary object. The distinction is between energy expended by the person and work done on the specified object.

Prelims focus

  • For a constant force acting along displacement, \(W=Fs\).
  • The SI unit of work is joule (J); \(1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
  • Work is positive when force and displacement have the same direction.
  • Work is negative when force and displacement have opposite directions.
  • Work by a perpendicular force is zero.
  • Trap: Physical effort or tiredness does not necessarily mean that mechanical work has been done on an object.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, 'Work and Energy', Sections 11.1.1–11.1.3, printed pp. 146–148, 2018–19 text; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 12, 'Friction', printed pp. 146–149.]

title: Work in Physics: Force, Displacement and Direction

body:
Meaning of energy

A moving cricket ball can strike and displace a wicket. Water flowing through a channel can turn a wheel. A raised object can do work as it falls. These examples show that an object may possess the ability to produce motion or bring about a change.

Energy is the capacity to do work. Its SI unit is the joule (J), the same unit used for work.

Energy and work are closely related but are not identical concepts. Energy describes a capacity or a quantity possessed by a system, whereas work describes a way of transferring energy when a force causes displacement. If a person lifts a book, work done against gravity increases the book's gravitational potential energy. If a moving ball strikes another object, some of the ball's energy can be transferred to that object.

A larger unit of energy is the kilojoule (kJ):

\(1\,\mathrm{kJ}=1000\,\mathrm{J}\)

Mechanical energy

The energy associated with an object's motion or position is called mechanical energy. It has 2 principal forms.

  • Kinetic energy: Energy possessed because an object is moving. Examples include a rolling ball, flowing water and a moving bicycle.
  • Potential energy: Energy possessed because of an object's position or configuration. Examples include a stone raised above the ground, a stretched rubber band and a compressed spring.

The total mechanical energy of an object or system is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies:

\(E_{\mathrm{mechanical}}=E_k+E_p\)

A falling stone may possess both forms simultaneously: it is moving and it is still above the ground. Therefore, kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy are not always mutually exclusive.

Other important forms of energy

Energy is not confined to moving objects and raised objects. Several forms are encountered in everyday life.

  • Chemical energy: Energy associated with substances such as food, fuels and the chemicals inside a battery.
  • Electrical energy: Energy transferred or supplied through electrical processes, such as that used by an electric fan or lamp.
  • Thermal energy: Energy associated with the random motion of the particles of matter. It is involved in heating and cooling.
  • Light energy: Energy carried by light, including sunlight.
  • Sound energy: Energy carried by sound waves, such as those produced by a vibrating bell.

Energy can be stored and later used

A wind-up toy provides an example. When a person turns its key, energy is transferred to a spring inside the toy. The spring stores energy because its shape has been changed. On releasing the mechanism, the stored potential energy can become kinetic energy as the toy moves.

Similarly, food contains chemical energy that the body uses to support movement and other life processes. A battery stores chemical energy and can supply electrical energy to a connected device. These examples show how energy can be stored, transferred and converted between forms.

An energy form is not the same as an energy source. Sunlight is a form of energy arriving from the Sun, while the Sun is its source. A battery is an energy-storage device containing chemicals; electrical energy is supplied when the battery operates in a circuit.

Prelims focus

  • Energy is the capacity to do work.
  • The SI unit of energy is joule (J).
  • \(1\,\mathrm{kJ}=1000\,\mathrm{J}\).
  • Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies.
  • Potential energy may be stored through position or change of shape.
  • Trap: Work and energy have the same SI unit, but work is a transfer of energy rather than a separate stored form of energy.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, 'Work and Energy', Sections 11.2 and 11.2.1, printed pp. 149–150, and Section 11.2.3, printed p. 152, 2018–19 text.]

title: Energy: Capacity to Do Work and Its Different Forms

body:
Energy possessed by a moving object

A moving cricket ball can displace a wicket when it strikes it. A stream of flowing water can turn a wheel, and a moving bicycle can push against an obstacle. In each case, motion gives the object the capacity to do work.

Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object because of its motion.

The kinetic energy of an object depends on its mass and speed. For an object of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\), its kinetic energy is:

$$E_k=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

Here, \(m\) is measured in kilograms (kg), \(v\) in metres per second (m/s), and \(E_k\) in joules (J).

Dependence on mass

When 2 objects move at the same speed, the object with greater mass has greater kinetic energy. For example, if 2 objects have masses of 2 kg and 4 kg and each moves at 3 m/s, their kinetic energies are:

\(E_{k1}=\frac12\times2\times3^2=9\,\mathrm{J}\)

\(E_{k2}=\frac12\times4\times3^2=18\,\mathrm{J}\)

Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy when speed remains unchanged. The relationship between kinetic energy and mass is therefore direct.

Dependence on speed

Speed has a stronger effect because it is squared in the formula. For an object whose mass stays constant:

  • Doubling its speed makes its kinetic energy 4 times as great.
  • Tripling its speed makes its kinetic energy 9 times as great.
  • Reducing its speed to half makes its kinetic energy one-fourth as great.

This explains why an increase in the speed of a moving vehicle produces a much larger increase in its kinetic energy, even when the vehicle's mass remains the same.

Calculating the effect of speed

A 2 kg object initially moves at 2 m/s.

\(E_k=\frac12\times2\times2^2=4\,\mathrm{J}\)

If its speed increases to 4 m/s without any change in mass:

\(E_k=\frac12\times2\times4^2=16\,\mathrm{J}\)

The speed has doubled, but kinetic energy has increased from 4 J to 16 J.

Connection between work and kinetic energy

When a force speeds up an object, the object gains kinetic energy. When a force slows it down, the object loses kinetic energy. The net work done by all forces on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

\(W_{\mathrm{net}}=E_{k,\mathrm{final}}-E_{k,\mathrm{initial}}\)

For example, if an object's kinetic energy rises from 4 J to 16 J, the net work done on it is +12 J. If braking reduces its kinetic energy from 16 J to 4 J, the net work done is −12 J.

An object at rest has zero kinetic energy because its speed is zero. Kinetic energy cannot be negative in this school-level expression because mass is nonnegative and speed is squared. The change in kinetic energy, however, can be negative.

Direction and speed are different. Kinetic energy depends on the magnitude of velocity, which is speed. If an object reverses direction but keeps the same speed and mass, its kinetic energy remains unchanged.

Prelims focus

  • \(E_k=\frac12mv^2\).
  • The SI unit of kinetic energy is joule (J).
  • At a fixed speed, kinetic energy is directly proportional to mass.
  • At a fixed mass, kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed.
  • Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.
  • Trap: Doubling speed makes kinetic energy 4 times as great, not 2 times as great.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, 'Work and Energy', Section 11.2.2, printed pp. 149–152, 2018–19 text; CBSE, Grade 9, Essential Concepts | Science, 'Work and Energy', consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Doubling speed increases kinetic energy by a factor of 4 when mass is unchanged.

title: Kinetic Energy: How Mass and Speed Affect Energy

body:
What is potential energy?

An object need not be moving to possess energy. A stone held above the ground can do work when released. A stretched rubber band can produce motion when released. In each case, energy has been stored because of the object's position or changed configuration.

Potential energy is energy possessed by an object or system because of its position or configuration.

At this level, 2 important examples are gravitational potential energy and elastic potential energy. They have different physical causes, although both can be converted into kinetic energy.

Gravitational potential energy

When a person lifts a book, a force is applied against gravity. The work done in raising the book increases its gravitational potential energy. Near Earth's surface, where gravitational acceleration can be treated as approximately constant, the increase in gravitational potential energy is:

$$E_p=mgh$$

Here, \(m\) is the object's mass in kg, \(g\) is acceleration due to gravity in m/s2, and \(h\) is the vertical height above a chosen reference level in m. The resulting potential energy is measured in joules.

For elementary calculations near Earth's surface, \(g\) is approximately 9.8 m/s2. Many school-level problems explicitly instruct students to use 10 m/s2 for easier arithmetic. Use the value specified in the problem.

Worked example: lifting a book

A 2 kg object is raised vertically through 3 m. Taking \(g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\):

\(E_p=mgh=2\times10\times3=60\,\mathrm{J}\)

Its gravitational potential energy increases by 60 J.

For a given value of \(g\), doubling the mass doubles the potential energy at the same height. Similarly, doubling the height doubles the potential energy of the same object.

Why the reference level matters

The height in the expression \(mgh\) is measured from a chosen reference level. If the floor is taken as zero height, an object resting on the floor has zero gravitational potential energy relative to that floor. This does not mean the object can never possess gravitational potential energy relative to another level.

For instance, a book on a table has positive gravitational potential energy relative to the floor but zero gravitational potential energy if the tabletop itself is chosen as the reference level. The difference in potential energy between 2 heights is the physically useful quantity.

Vertical height, not distance travelled

If a person carries a load from the ground to the same upper level using a ramp instead of lifting it vertically, the increase in gravitational potential energy is still \(mgh\), provided the starting and ending heights are the same. It is the vertical change in height, not the length of the path, that determines this change.

Gravity acts downward. Consequently, when an object rises, gravity does negative work on it. When the object falls, gravity does positive work on it.

Elastic potential energy

A stretched rubber band, compressed spring or bent bow stores energy because its shape has been changed. This is called elastic potential energy. When the object returns towards its original shape, some of this stored energy may become kinetic energy.

For example, winding the spring of a toy car stores potential energy. Releasing the mechanism allows the spring to drive the toy. Unlike gravitational potential energy, this energy depends on deformation rather than height above the ground.

The expression \(E_p=mgh\) applies to gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface. It is not a formula for every type of potential energy, including that stored in a stretched rubber band.

Prelims focus

  • Potential energy can arise from position or configuration.
  • Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is \(E_p=mgh\).
  • The SI unit of potential energy is joule (J).
  • Gravitational potential energy depends on the chosen reference level.
  • Work done against gravity raises gravitational potential energy.
  • Trap: In \(mgh\), \(h\) is vertical height, not the total distance travelled along a path.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, 'Work and Energy', Sections 11.2.3–11.2.4, printed pp. 152–153, 2018–19 text.]

title: Potential Energy: Energy Stored by Position or Shape
